utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Edgerton, since you're standing, may I take it that you'll examine the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you ready to call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's Elvir Jahic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put in your microphone, yes. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, Your Honour, I can indicate that Mr. Stewart won't be here today, and Ms. Cmeric won't be here today either. Ms. Cmeric has had to return to Belgrade. She will be back, I think, on Wednesday afternoon. In the meantime, of course, that means we won't have, on the part of the Defence, a B/C/S speaker in the courtroom. That, of course, requires some adjustment in terms of our ability to speak with Mr. Krajisnik during the break. And I've made some arrangements with the Registry in relation to having a translator available, but of course, we may require slightly longer breaks to communicate with Mr. Krajisnik and matters of that sort. And I just put that on the record so Your Honours are aware of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that under these circumstances you will need other practical arrangements. It was last Friday when it was announced that Ms. Cmeric really needed a few days off. Then the witness came in. Otherwise we would have wished her a few nice days after a lot of hard work. But since the witness was then entering the courtroom, I thought that it was not appropriate. So that was what was on my mind last Friday, and you could perhaps communicate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I'm sure that it was not only on my mind, but also on the mind of the Chamber as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, and I'll certainly communicate that to Ms. Cmeric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Jahic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jahic. Please be seated. Mr. Jahic, Ms. Edgerton, who is counsel for the Prosecution, will examine you first. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton Examined by Ms. Edgerton:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jahic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jahic.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, as we begin, I'd just like to ask you a little bit of background information about yourself and where you're from. I understand you were born in the settlement of Ahatovici and have spent most of your life there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us which municipality Ahatovici is located in.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Ahatovici is a settlement belonging to the Novi Grad municipality of Sarajevo, which means it is a suburb of Sarajevo, on the periphery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say on the periphery, could you give us an idea of approximately how far Ahatovici is from the Sarajevo city centre, for example.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Ahatovici is at a distance of approximately 15 kilometres from the centre of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, perhaps you could tell us about the size of the settlement itself. For example, could you give us an idea how many family homes were located in the settlement in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: In Ahatovici, there were approximately 100 or, rather, 100 to 120 family homes, and they were inhabited predominantly by the Muslim population. In percentage terms, more than 90 per cent were Muslims, Muslims living in Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what about the settlements and areas adjoining and surrounding Ahatovici settlement? Were those mainly Muslim or Serb or mixed settlements?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: The surrounding Ahatovici settlements were Dobrosevici, Bojnik Mihajlevici, Rajlovac, Belugovici, Reljevo, and some of these settlements were inhabited by a majority Serb population, whereas in one or two of the settlements that I enumerated, there was a mixed population. Some were Bosnian Serbs, some others were Bosnian Croats, and there were some Muslims and other ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, of the list that you've just given us, could you identify which settlements or areas were mixed.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: In Bojnik, for instance, you had a mixed population. And in Dobrosevici, as well, and Mihajlevici too. But percentage-wise, it was the -- the majority population were the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other settlements that you've enumerated, then, including Reljevo and Rajlovac, were majority Serb population; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any JNA facilities in the area of your settlement?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. For example, on the local commune of Dobrosevici, under which Ahatovici comes, there were two barracks, in fact, belonging to the former Yugoslav People's Army, or more specifically, in Butile, which is to the south-west of Ahatovici. And in Rajlovac as well, there was another barracks, which was an air force barracks and anti-air attack premises. And that is south-east of Ahatovici. There was another barracks which was located in Ilijas, the Ilijas municipality. It was very close to Ahatovici, not that far away from Ahatovici. And it was to the north-west of Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of that barracks, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after that background information, could I take you directly to the period leading up to the takeover of your settlement in 1992. First, I'd like to ask you: Can you recall any event which resulted in this serious limitation of freedom of movement of the people of your settlement?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, this is what happened: Immediately before the attack on Ahatovici, or the aggression launched against Ahatovici, my village and the surrounding settlements was engulfed with a wartime psychosis. There was a mood that prevailed that was like that. And this affected celebrations and festivities, for example, the festivities that were organised by the Serb inhabitants, our neighbours, for example. There would be a lot of nationalistic songs sung, and songs which directly had a threatening note and message to us Muslims in Ahatovici. They were songs -- for instance, one was a song about Topola, and another called Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the Chetniks to rally and organise, for example. And another one was about a young Turkish girl who swore in front of a mosque that she only loved Serbs. And as far as restriction of movement was concerned -- actually, the position of Ahatovici is such that from the city of Sarajevo, it is separated by the Bosna River, which had two bridges. There were two bridges which would let you reach the town of Sarajevo. And these two bridges had been taken control of by the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can just stop you there and ask you: Do you recall at what time, approximately, those bridges had been occupied or taken control of?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, give you an exact date when it all started, but I assume a rough guess would be that it began one or two months prior to the beginning of the aggression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just speaking about the bridges being taken control of, can you tell us how they were taken control of?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. What happened was that barricades were erected, with several machine-gun nests, and the hedgehog devices were erected. There was general control of the area, so you couldn't reach the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did those barricades you've just described remain in place from the time of the erection until the takeover of your settlement?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who manned those barricades?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: On two or three occasions, I personally tried to cross those barricades, because there was -- the shops in Ahatovici were not well supplied with food and other goods, cigarettes, for example, and other staples. So I tried to reach Sarajevo to buy cigarettes, for example, and some food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened when you tried to cross those barricades.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: I was stopped by some people. I knew some of them, but not others. And for me to be able to cross over into Sarajevo, they asked me to sign a loyalty oath to the Republika Srpska. That was a condition that they laid down. And I had my doubts, because there were previous events in which people were arrested and taken to camps, for example. So I was a bit wary. That was the condition they set. But I wasn't able to pass through the barricades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said when you went to those barricades, you recognised some people. Do you recall their names?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: I recall some of them. I recognised some of my friends from school, for example, schoolmates who were there up at the barricades. I don't know whether they were on duty there, but I saw them. They were people who lived in the settlement of Bojnik, for example, and perhaps some of them were from Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, also in this period leading up to the attack on your village, did you observe any physical activity going on around the outside of the settlement which might have led you to be concerned for the safety of yourself or your fellow residents?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just before the aggression on Ahatovici, all the inhabitants of Ahatovici, all of us, were able to see that the regular army, that is to say the Yugoslav People's Army, had left the area around the barracks which I mentioned in my statement. And a lot of the local inhabitants, the Bosnian Serbs, left to join up the reserve formations of the Yugoslav People's Army. And then they started fortifying themselves. They started amassing heavy weapons around Ahatovici, in Paljevo, Tjepovac, those were the areas where this took place. And in some private houses as well. For example, the Koprivica houses and the Torbica houses. What was happening, in actual fact, as far as we were able to see and gather, was that this was heavy weaponry, mostly Howitzers, cannons and tanks, with their barrels turned on Ahatovici. And 90 per cent of the population, as well as myself, led us to realise that Ahatovici was going to be attacked, that there was an aggression being prepared against Ahatovici and an attack against Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can just stop you for a second and go back and ask you a couple of questions about what you've just described. Let's talk first of all about the departure of the regular army from the barracks you've previously identified.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself see the departure of the regular army?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you saw.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw columns of military vehicles, trucks, APCs, larger ones, smaller ones, and they were moving along the road from Bojnik to Stup, roughly speaking. They were going off somewhere. I didn't know where they were going to. But this led me to think that they were leaving those military facilities, pulling out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you just tell us where Stup is in relation to Bojnik and the Sarajevo city centre.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, Stup is to the north of Ahatovici. Yes. We could say it was north, because there's Bojnik and it's at the entrance to the city of Sarajevo itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned something you described as fortifying. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, the heavy weapons from the barracks, from that barracks or some other barracks around Sarajevo, they dug these fortifications with dredges and the Howitzers and guns and cannons were being entrenched in this area of Rajlovac towards Bojnik and we could see them digging in, that they were pulling out the tanks and making a sort of shelter for those tanks and the barrels of all the weaponry that I mentioned were turned on Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I could ask you: As a result of everything you've just described, did you or any others take any steps that you thought might ease the tensions?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know exactly how much time before the attack, the direct attack on Ahatovici, a group of about 10 or 12 - I can't give you an exact number - of Ahatovici locals, and I was among them, went to the Butile barracks, and our purpose in going there was to join up with the reserve formation of the then Yugoslav People's Army, to have a more mixed composition for the army and to come by some weapons. Because we realised that an attack, an aggression, was being prepared against Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened when you went to Butile barracks?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: After a brief conversation with the commander of the barracks - I can't remember his name just now - and his position was categoric; he said -- he found a pretext and said that -- and gave us a reason why we couldn't join up with the reserve formation of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask him why not?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: I can't remember what he said. A lot of time has gone by since then. It's been 12 years, 1992, and it's 2004 now, so you can see for yourself. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time as well, do you recall having heard anything in the media, for example, of events in other areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, via the media, we were able to hear that in Eastern Bosnia, for example, and in some other towns, that the population had been slaughtered, more precisely, in Foca, Bijeljina, et cetera, Zvornik, not to mention some other towns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As time drew closer to the attack on your settlement, did you receive any information of events in neighbouring or nearby non-Serb settlements?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, we had some information which later turned out to be correct, namely, that in Semizovac, in Surake, nearby populated areas, a lot of people had already been killed or taken to camps, and that there was a large number of troops, including Seselj's men and some other paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just tell us where Surake and Semizovac are located.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Surake and Semizovac belong to Vogosca municipality, and they are Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond to the north-east of Ahatovici. The distances may be 20 to 30 kilometres as the crow flies, roughly. I can't be precise. But please don't take my word for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection now of how you received this information about events in Surake and Semizovac?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Through the media, and also from people who somehow managed to flee and to reach free territory. Those people told others about what had happened in their villages and the villages around them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As things were building up, then, did you and other members of your settlement make any effort to save certain members of the population of the settlement, to evacuate them?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. It was maybe ten days before the direct, all-out attack on Ahatovici. We tried to pull out women, children, and the elderly, with the idea of following them later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you try to do that?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, within Ahatovici, we organised a couple of men who owned trucks, vans, and similar vehicles, and at a certain point - I don't know exactly at which time - all the civilian population started moving out, using this transportation, towards Visoko municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Visoko municipality lay in what direction in relation to Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: To the north-west, if I'm not mistaken, from Ahatovici. It was a road little used; in fact, a track through the woods. Up to a certain point you could drive, but there was a large section of the track where you had to go on foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said you weren't sure exactly what time this group set out, but could you maybe give us an idea if this was in the daytime or in the evening? Was it light or dark outside?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: They set out early in the morning. It could have been 6.30, 7.00 a.m. That convoy set out very early in the morning from Ahatovici, and then at the exit from Ahatovici, near a place called Torbica, they were stopped by those Serb neighbours of ours, led by Jovo Torbica. He smirked at those people - I know this because I was escorting the convoy - and said to them: Where are you headed, neighbours? Is something going on? And there was a lot of cynicism and irony in his voice. The convoy was able to pass through, nevertheless, and they continued on to Bioci, B-i-o-c-i -- B-i-o-c-a, sorry, but they couldn't go on. They had to dismount the vehicles and continue on foot, the women and the children. Then, when they reached the locality of Crni Potoci, which belongs to the Ilijas municipality, this convoy of about 150 women, children, and the elderly came under machine-gun fire. I don't think the idea was to kill those people, but it was the idea to make it clear to them they had to turn back so that this attempt by civilians to leave Ahatovici was unsuccessful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they then do that? Did they turn back?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of anybody injured or killed as a result of the machine-gun fire?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to escorting this convoy, did you have any close family members who were a part of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There was the wife of my late brother, who got killed, and her baby, around 12 months old. I also had a lot of close and not-so-close relatives in that convoy. I don't want to enumerate them here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to trying to evacuate civilians, did you do anything else, you or the other residents of your settlement, to prepare for an impending attack?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Since we were left to our own devices and unable to leave in the direction of Sarajevo or Visoko, we were completely encircled, and therefore, we tried to organise some sort of self-defence in order to prevent a massacre of this population. We tried to protect them. And for that purpose, we got hold of some weapons, mainly light infantry weapons, a couple of rifles, a couple of improvised devices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get hold of those weapons?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, some people from Ahatovici had purchased their weapons, which was possible, just before things started happening. I don't know where exactly they bought them, but I know weapons could be bought, up to a certain time. Some of the weapons came from the Territorial Defence of Visoko, but I stress again: It was only a couple of rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talk about improvised devices, could you tell us what you mean by those.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, those were self-made rifles of certain profile that could use hunting ammunition. Do-it-yourself rifles, basically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a part of this self-organised defence, as you call it, how many were you? What number of people were in this self-organised defence?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: In Ahatovici, there were a hundred to 120 able-bodied men of military age at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those only men from Ahatovici or did they come from areas as well?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: At the outset, those were the natives of Ahatovici, the locals, people who lived there, plus maybe 20 men from other municipalities. There was, for instance, a group of 12 men from Bratunac municipality who, by sheer chance and in ended up in Ahatovici, while trying to escape. Those were former prisoners of the bat Bratunac and Pale camps. They were in extremely bad shape, mentally and physically. Some of them had broken ribs. They were generally black and blue from beatings with skin covered with cuts from the beatings in the camps at Pale and in Bratunac. Some of them had the four S symbol carved into their skin. I think you could see that on some documentaries that were made since. As for people -- or rather, men from Bioca, they ended up in Ahatovici while fleeing desperately from Bioca, trying to save their lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm not sure if we've covered this, but Bioca is located in which municipality? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: One part of Bioca, to be more precise, Gornja Bioca, belongs to our municipality, the municipality of Novi Grad, whereas lower Bioca, or Donja Bioca, belongs to Ilijas municipality. It's a place where a large number of male population above 18 ended up in camps, and some of them were even incinerated in the smelter, or rather, in the ironworks of Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So protectors of your settlement came from Ahatovici, Bratunac, and Bioca?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe there were 95 men from Ahatovici, so that number includes a total of 100 to 120 men in Ahatovici, including 12 from Bratunac. I cannot be more precise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could just talk about these men from Bratunac again. Did you receive any information as to how these men had gotten out of detention from Bratunac? And how, in fact, they made their way to your settlement?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, from what they told us, they were captured in Bratunac and they had to go through terrible things before they were imprisoned in a gym-like centre, detention centre, in Pale, to be exchanged in Visoko in May 1992. I had the opportunity to see some of those people on TV, and some of those people later reached us, and they told us how they were attacked without any provocation or reason how many men were taken away to camps, and those men had to go through a Golgotha.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: And as for the second part of your question, they arrived together with a group of about ten men, ten local men who had received some weapons from Territorial Defence in Visoko. They received those light infantry weapons from the TO in Visoko, and then through those woods that I described, they managed to reach Ahatovici. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned you had seen these men who originated in Bratunac on television. Could you just tell us the circumstances of seeing them on television? What was the nature of the report, if that was that, that you saw?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: It was a report on the BH television, on the Sarajevo television, about their exchange in Visoko. And it showed the condition of these people. It showed the cuts on their skin, their broken arms and legs, their emaciation. They showed, in particular, one man who had spent a lot of time in that camp. They were undernourished, physically and mentally exhausted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would say that this draws us to the time immediately before the attack on your settlement. In the days immediately before the attack, did the people of Ahatovici see anything that might have led them to believe an attack was imminent?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: I saw with my own eyes, just as a lot of people from Ahatovici saw it, in a report from Belgrade TV, this depiction of Ahatovici as a stronghold of Green Berets, where a lot of Green Berets were just waiting to mount an attack on the surrounding villages that I mentioned at the beginning of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, being there in Ahatovici at the time, was that the case?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: No. It was propaganda. They were probably looking for an excuse before the international community for something that was going to happen in Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your settlement, were you able to see any events going on in the adjoining settlements that led you to believe that an attack would be imminent?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I watched the attack from the Rajlovac barracks against the Sokolje populated area, which had a Muslim-majority population, with my own eyes, and I also watched the attack on Otes, mounted from the barracks in Butile. I believe artillery weapons were used in that attack. And for the most part, those attacks were mounted in the evening hours, after dark. Those populated areas were also shelled from Paljevo. They were targeted by Howitzers, and we could see the mosque on Sokolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us where Sokolje is in relation to Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: It's east of Ahatovici, or south-east, roughly, in the direction of the Rajlovac barracks, along the same axis as Rajlovac barracks, just a bit further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is Otes?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: The Otes populated area belongs to Ilidza municipality, and it is located to the north -- sorry, to the south of Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is Paljevo?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: To the north of Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This, I think, moves us forward in time to the attack on your settlement. Could you tell us about that. Could you begin with the date at which it took place.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: The attack on Ahatovici, as far as I know, happened on the 25th of May, 1992, and I believe this date is correct. First, without any provocation or cause, infantry fire was opened on Ahatovici and continued all day, until sunrise, when artillery fire started pounding incessantly from the localities that I already mentioned. It was a huge number of shells, between a thousand and 1.200 shells every day, of different calibres. Also, some incendiary shells and some fragmentation ammunition was used, which I believe are forbidden by Geneva Conventions, so that many houses in Ahatovici burnt down. Even before that, electricity and water supply had been cut off, so we were unable to even try to put out the fire on those houses. We could just watch, helplessly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the fire came from the localities that you've mentioned, could you be more specific. What direction was fire coming from?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, the firing came from the area around Rajlovac, or more precisely, the locality of the city -- and there were tanks, mortars, Howitzers, from the localities of Tjepovac, for example, Paljevo and there was infantry fire or machine-gun fire also from the trenches that were dug, that had been dug. And I think I said in my statement where those trenches were located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I just ask you: You mentioned the word collect, and I didn't hear anything after that. Could you tell us what you were talking about. "The city collect ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Collector or reservoir, interpreter's note, but the witness can explain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I can ask you in a different way. What were you talking about when you said one of the places the fire was coming from was the city collect?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Ah, yes. The word "collector," I meant -- I'm talking about the sewage system for the city of Sarajevo, and where the sewage was collected and filtered and then sent further on down the Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did that lie in relation to your settlement?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: To the south-east, near the Rajlovac barracks, about one or two kilometres away from the Rajlovac barracks, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you've described what sounds to me like very intensive shelling that began the day following the initial attack. How long did that go on for?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, the attacks were continuous from the 29th of May, 1992 until the 2nd of June, the fall of Ahatovici, in fact, also in 1992. So it was that period. Five to six days, or however much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What had happened meanwhile to the people who had been -- the women and children who had been turned back from their attempt at evacuation?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Most of the children, the women and children and elderly, were put up in a house which we considered to be, by virtue of its position, the most suitable for putting up a shelter there. And that is where about 150 people were put up, women, children, and elderly persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any close family members in that shelter?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] Da.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had my brother's wife, with a baby that was a year old. There was my father, who, just prior to the aggression, had had an operation. He was with them there. And I think there were a lot of other people who ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware or did you receive any information of any persons killed or injured as a result of this period of shelling?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any information about that. Actually, I do remember one particular case. It was a boy, a minor. He might have been 12 at the time, perhaps, who was hit in the area of his stomach. And some other people too who received light wounds during the shelling. But I should also like to say that the Chetniks knew about the shelter and that they targeted the shelter continuously too, from the locality that I did not mention, but it was by the reservoir, the water reservoir, which is situated south of Ahatovici, between, roughly speaking, the barracks and Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Is the water reservoir the same as the city collector, or something additional?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: No. It's something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lying in approximately the same location?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: The water reservoir is closer to the Ahatovici settlement, if we look at the location of this city collector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that the attack continued until about 2nd of June. Could you tell us what happened and what happened to you on that date.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of June, 1992, our defence, the defence of the Ahatovici settlement, could no longer resist the attacks launched by the Chetniks, so that they managed to break through our defence lines at three or four places, and they started entering the Ahatovici settlement, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond together with a group of about -- or several people who were members of the Territorial Defence of Ahatovici. I don't want to say -- or rather, we had to withdraw to the interior of Ahatovici to prevent them from coming at us from behind. And we wanted to try and break through to the people who were in the other part of Ahatovici. During this breakthrough, we were noticed, they noticed us, and they started firing at us continuously, using heavy weaponry, machine-gun fire. And on that occasion when we were trying to break through towards the Ranovaci area, two people were killed from that group. They were Avdo Gacanovic and Saban Ibrahim [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could stop you for a moment so we could go back a little bit in time. You said: "They managed to break through our defence lines at three or four places." I take it by that you're talking -- you're referring to the aggressor forces?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see them break through and enter the settlement?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, from the Dobrosevici direction, with two APCs. They were moving along the road, towards the shelter where the women and children and elderly were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dobrosevici lies in which direction in relation to your settlement?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Dobrosevici, too, is to the south-east of Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you described that you -- your attempted breakthrough towards the Ranovaci area, could you tell us which direction you're heading in.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Ranovaci, yes. It's north-west of Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, if I just may interrupt you for one second. We've heard some -- almost 15 to 20 questions about which was north of what, relative geographical positions are very difficult to memorise without the help of a map. It would have saved you a lot of questions if you just could see it on a map, where this village is in relation to another one. So it would certainly assist the Chamber to have an overview map so we could more easily follow the witness. The second observation I'd like to make is you used the word aggressor forces and I am aware the witness used similar terms, but the Chamber is more assisted by knowing who that means, Serbian or paramilitary or BH force, whatever. That assists us better in making the determinations we finally have to make. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could go back, then, to your attempted breakthrough towards Visoko area. Could you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, we managed, after about an hour of crawling, suffering certain casualties, or rather, the people who I said were killed on the occasion, we managed to get to Ranovaci and join up with our people who were in that area. At that point in time, it was a group of about 50.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With that group of about 50, did you then take any action? What then did you do?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: We tried to continue breaking through to the hill of Krstac. We thought that we could go over the hill, the Krstac hill and through the forest and then that we might have a chance of reaching Visoko that way. In the meantime, the Chetniks had taken control of the largest portion of Ahatovici and the place the civilians were, where the women and children were located, that too. On that occasion they used a megaphone and appealed to us to surrender. They said: Balijas, surrender yourselves or we'll kill your women and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of that, did you then do anything?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: After holding brief consultations between us and that group of 50 people, we discussed the situation and we made some decisions. We said that if we surrendered, many of us would be killed, if not all of us. So what we decided was to try and break through the other way, the breakthrough we had discussed previously, and that's what we managed to do. While we were breaking through, we had to come out on to an open space, 50 metres, dividing Krstac hill and the first nearby house, where we were. When we had to run across this open space, while we were doing that, about 20 people were killed in a very short space of time, because we were exposed to repeated shelling, cross-fire from an APC and from the machine-guns. So as I say, 20 people were killed during that attempt, more than 10 person are listed missing and they haven't been found to this day. I myself was in the group of men who surrendered to the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you: Do you recall the names of any of those 20 people who were killed?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Among those Chetniks I recognised my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Perhaps I should repeat my question, Mr. Jahic. You might not have understood me. I asked: Do you recall the names of any of those 20 people who were killed?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They were all people whom I knew, my schoolmates, good friends of mine. Their names -- do you want me to give you their names?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ones that you recall, please.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: There was Samir Mujkic, Dokman Nihad, Suljic Jusuf, Divovic Hamko one of the Mesanovic brothers, I don't remember his name. There were two brothers and both of them were killed. They were twins, in fact, whether it was Nihad or Nedzad, I'm not quite sure. Then there was Becir Zigac and two other men with the same surname, Zigac. I can't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the other names just now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. Now, as a result of seeing this that had gone on before you, did you then decide to do anything?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: I was in a group of people -- with a group of men. I was right at the back, in the rear. So it was sort of an assignment I had to protect this attempt at breakthrough, and together with my brother -- I was together with my brother, but we were noticed. The Chetniks noticed us and they used the megaphone to tell us to surrender. We had no other -- no way out, no other choice, and had to surrender.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was your surrender effected?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, we were given instructions through the megaphone to raise our arms high up above our heads and to start moving towards the others, the other men who had surrendered. Among them there were quite a number of wounded. And we had to cross an area of about 30 metres to reach those other people, with our hands raised up. We started out, started moving, according to the instructions we were given, towards those men, and then they opened fire at us, or rather, from our neighbour's houses, Koprivica, they opened fire. And we had to throw ourselves down on the ground not to be hit. And another Chetnik with a megaphone cursed our balija mothers, swore at us, and ordered us to get up off the ground and to move towards him. We tried to get up with our arms raised again and we tried to reach the place the other prisoners were, but they started shooting at us again. So once again we had to throw ourselves down onto the ground. Another time -- the second time we got up, we somehow managed to reach that other group. I don't know how many prisoners there were there from Ahatovici exactly, but we managed to reach that group and the Chetniks that had taken them prisoner, and then we were ordered to lie down, face down, face towards the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, who gave you that order?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: The person with the megaphone. I didn't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he wearing any kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: All those people whom I saw and recognised, some of them were wearing uniform -- either uniforms of the reserve formation of the former JNA or the uniforms of the members of the air force institute at Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the uniforms of the members of the air force institute at Rajlovac different in any way from those of the reserve JNA?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were blue trousers, or overalls, and light-blue shirts, whereas the other type of uniform, the reservist JNA uniforms, were green, or rather, olive-green. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea or could you estimate approximately how many people there in uniform you saw all together?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: As we were in the position we were in, we weren't able to see round about. We had to lie down on the ground. I just managed to see about a hundred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among those 100, did you recognise anyone that you had known previously?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I was able to recognise someone. Our next-door neighbours, for instance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us their names, the names of those that you recall having recognised.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: I remember seeing in that group Davor and Bato Arnautovic. They were brothers. I saw them clearly. Then there was Goran and Zoran Zdralo, also brothers; Braco Mirkovic, Marinko Simeunovic, Pero Koprivica, Dalibor Koprivica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know the --

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: And some others, if you want me to give you some more names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnicity of these people who you've just named?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: All the people I named were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton. We'll have a break. But I'd first like to ask Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, do you think that -- this witness is scheduled for three hours, as far as I remember, on the last list. I also noticed that a lot of details are coming in. I mean, it would have been -- if a witness says that he recognised some of his locals and neighbours, would we really ask him for 60 seconds to find all the names? Of course if there would be any doubt on whether this recollection is correct or not, I take it that in cross-examination, then Ms. Loukas would try to establish that this recognition of locals is not correct. We have similar experiences this morning. Also I wondered, for example, why quite many details about what happened in the defence activities, why couldn't hold the lines, where they finally tried to break through, where they lost -- whether there were some casualties in the group the witness was in. And then finally, they couldn't escape any more and -- I don't know whether that really needs 50 minutes. I mean, that's not the core of your case, is it? It's not what happened exactly in these combat activities. So my question is whether you think you could finish within the time or from what I noticed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just advised by Mr. Hannis that in the last, most recent estimate of time for this witness, he's set for four hours, rather than three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then just look at -- I don't know whether you have any more recent one, but I've got the 29th of October, 2004, which gives us an estimate of three hours. And, well, then I see the exhibits. The exhibit list, by the way, is from another date. It's from the 26th of October, and still mentions Prnjavor municipality rather than Novi Sarajevo. I take it that's a small mistake. But if you have any more recent one than the 29th, then ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think I'm advised on an earlier list he was listed for four hours. He's since been changed to three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That might solve things. And I'm advised it should have read four. The intention was that it should read four hours. And that's my estimate of the time he would be taking, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Of course, I'm also thinking about the Thursday and Friday not being available. I don't know whether we can get through our witnesses. But I wonder whether -- it also struck me that on some aspects, at least, that this witness was not been presented as an 89(F) witness which, at least in respect of some of his testimony of the last one hour and a half, might have been appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was in fact a call, but because there were so many previous statements from the witness, I had made the decision to call him viva voce, having recourse to his previous statements only if there was a need to refresh his recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I don't anticipate with the way things are going that that's going to be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we'll have a break until 12.00. The Chamber still hopes --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 11.00, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 11.00. Yes, yes. On this clock until 12.00, but this clock has not yet been adapted to the wintertime. So it will be until 11.00. If the Chamber could receive a map of the area, it would certainly greatly assist in understanding the testimony. And if you would please keep in mind that we'd like to hear everything relevant, but in a way as efficient as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. I'd like to thank Your Honours for the indulgence of that additional ten minutes as we had to make quite some arrangements during the break as I foreshadowed to Your Honours, and I also understand that additional time enabled the Prosecution to get the map that you were addressing that question to Ms. Edgerton about. So all in all, I think it was relatively productive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One of the reasons why I asked for a map is also because the answer of the witness on whether Stup was located -- where he answered that Stup was located north of Ahatovici and I felt the need at that moment to check that on the map. If that answer might be in any way incorrect, could you please clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. What I think we'll do is go through the core evidence of his testimony and then go back to the map after that, if Your Honour agrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that would be necessary. It's just for us to follow where the river Bosna is, where it comes together with the ... But one specific answer might be -- might need some verification. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. So therefore, the Prosecutor is not invited to go through it again, because from what we know, general knowledge of geography of -- we had no other hesitations at this moment, but it's just easier to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, at the moment we broke --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, at the moment we broke, we were talking about your surrender to Serbs, some of whom you recognised.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: I can't hear very well. Yes, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We were talking about your surrender to Serbs in uniform, some of whom you recognised. Could you take up your story from that point and tell us what then happened to you, and what I'd like you to begin with is to tell us the approximate number of people you -- were who surrendered.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: It was a group of ten to twelve people. I don't know exactly how many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to you, Mr. Jahic?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: When we came to the place where we were invited to come and where the other detainees were, we were ordered to lie down, and then this man whom I didn't know, who had a radio station, a field radio on his back, an RUP radio station, was receiving instructions what to do with us. And in Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the meantime, one of those Chetniks who had captured us, Bato Arnautovic, set out to slit the throat of one man. He was holding a knife in his hand. And the name of the victim was Jusuf Suljic. I wasn't able to see whether he succeeded in that intention, but there was a man who was trying to stop him from cutting the throat of that man. It was Braco Mirkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, did you ever see Suljic alive after this time?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: No. This man Suljic was exhumed in 1996 in a mass grave in Ranovaci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, what -- could you tell us what then happened to the group of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: They ordered us to stand up and they tied us, two by two. They tied our hands. Each was tied to another man's hand with barbed wire. They took away all the weapons we had and emptied it of all ammunition and put the weapons back on our backs and made us go. We didn't know where we were going. We also had to carry wounded people. And there were two or three seriously wounded men. We were ordered to take a macadam road that went through the Klanac area, that went by Koprivica, towards Bojnik. And all the time that we were walking, they cursed our balija mothers. They called us names. They cursed the Bosnian president, Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Jahic. If I could just interrupt you there. Did you have to carry either wounded or weapons?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Both weapons and the wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the same time as you were tied to another prisoner with barbed wire?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "they" cursed you during your walk, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Those Chetniks who captured us and the people who used to be our neighbours until so recently, and they even stoned us on the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you stop?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: We stopped outside the little market in Bojnik, which was not far from the Butile barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened there?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Down there, we were able to see a large concentration of the Chetniks outside this shop, who were probably organised to carry out the torture that we were in for in Bojnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jahic, when you say "large concentration of Chetniks," could you describe in more detail the type of group you're talking about. What did you see?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: I saw uniformed men, some of which I was able to recognise because I had known them before. They were armed. There was also an armoured vehicle outside, an APC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say these men were uniformed, could you tell us what type of uniform you observed.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: There were several types of uniform, starting with JNA reservist uniforms and the blue uniforms of the air defence from Rajlovac, and there were some men in camouflage uniforms. They had some insignia. Some had the sign of the cross with the four S; some had a tricolour with JNA insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've said now that you've recognised some of these people. Could you tell us the ethnicity of those that you recognised.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: All of those whom I knew were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us an estimate as to the size of the total group of uniformed people who waited for you?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you an exact figure, but it was a large number, around a hundred men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything then happen to you in front of this supermarket?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. As we arrived outside this shop in Bojnik, they cut off the wire with which we had been tied, and they ordered us to undress to our underwear, to our shorts, and to lie down on the clearing outside the shop, which was made of stone, and to lie down spread-eagled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you were ordered to strip down to your underwear. What about your footwear? Did you still have that on?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: No. We had to take everything off except our shorts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what then happened to you?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: A filthy kind of torture began. We were hit with rifle butts, clubs, police truncheons. They hit us on the head with bottles. They used their hands and feet, whatever they could lay their hands on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything then happen to end this?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how much time elapsed, how much that torture lasted, an hour or maybe two, before a green military van arrived from the direction of Dobrosevici or somewhere - I wasn't able to tell - and some people got out of that van. They said that we were supposed to be taken to Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you get taken to Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: We were taken there by bus. But to make you see more clearly what happened in Bojnik, do you want me to give you the names of the people I knew? Because there were among them some former schoolmates of mine who tortured me and beat me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, if you would have a map meanwhile, then it might be a good idea already to ask the witness whether that covers the area he's talking about, so that we can more easily follow. But if you have not yet, then we'll have to wait.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could have your indulgence for just a moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the map sits behind me, but at this moment it's not yet mounted on anything to be able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have a big map, not -- you haven't --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's a large map, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I better do understand that ... If we could mount it on something.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And meanwhile, Your Honour, the witness's question was whether I'd like to receive the names of those people who were participating in the torture of them, of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, it's -- it's finally it's a matter for you, but of course you know that we have certain lists sometimes of names that are to be proven at some other moments. It's not that relevant. So I leave it entirely up to you. Now you have got a problem that you can't see the map any more, Ms. -- but perhaps we could for the cameras, we'll be able to solve that problem. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, if you can today recall the names of some of the people who you recognised who participated in this torture at Bojnik, could you please give those to us.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Out of that group, I recognised Damjanovic brothers, Goran, Zoran, and Vedran; Relja Dino; the son of Spasoje Sipanovic, whose name eludes me for the moment. Vera Hrkanovic. She was especially heavy-handed with us prisoners. And there was also her husband, Dragan, whose surname I can't recall now. And when I say Vera Hrkanovic, that's her maiden name, Hrkanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jahic. Now, you said you were taken from Bojnik to Rajlovac by bus.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the same bus that drove up before the supermarket?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the same bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any guards on this bus?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many guards there were. Maybe three to four, plus driver. Then we had to get up off that clearing, that plateau. And it was very hard to get up, because we were physically in very bad shape. And before that, the Chetniks who were there made a gauntlet for us to run through, some 20 metres long, 10 men on each side, and we, the detainees, had to run that gauntlet. And as we did so, we were hit again and again with rifles, wooden clubs, iron bars; we were slapped, kicked, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond hit with other objects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the bus ride to Rajlovac from Butile, I wonder if you could have a look --

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: From Bojnik to Rajlovac, you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct. I wonder if you could have a look at the map that's been produced to you and take a few moments and tell us if the map that you see before you displays the two locations we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to point? Here it is. That happened here. That's the little supermarket. And then we were taken by this road, passing through Mihajlevici, Belugovici, Reljevo, and then on to Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if at this point I could ask the witness with, I think, the blue pen he has in front of him, to mark that route on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you going to use -- you want to tender this -- is it a plastified map?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Marking on plastic is certainly possible. The problem, however, is that even on the screen, it's relatively small. You took a large map for a relatively small area. Wouldn't it be -- well, I'm just asking myself whether it would not be easier to have approximately 20 per cent of that map photocopied and then ask the witness to do that. Because otherwise we have a huge map which then should also be reproduced in similar size, which is, apart from that it takes a lot of time, it's also very expensive, especially if it's in colour. And it was just for our orientation. So I wonder whether not a more practical solution could be found. But of course ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, after the break, I think we'll be able to work better on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And marking as such. I mean, if you see on a map where Rajlovac is, and if you can follow what the witness says and if you just summarise that for the transcript, then the Judges are usually able to find their way on the maps. Because I'm afraid now that when I asked for a simple solution, the solution is more complex than the problem ever was. So please proceed, but I'd rather be hesitant to ask the witness to mark this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So during this trip to Rajlovac by bus, you've said you were under guard. There were guards on the bus, approximately three or four. Could you tell us if they were in uniform.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of uniform were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Blue trousers, light-blue shirts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the guards; and if so, can you comment on their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Later during my stay at the camp, I saw that man for the first time, and I continued to see him regularly throughout the time I was at the camp. He called himself and other people knew him as Sok. That was his nickname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: He was Serb, but he used a certain amount of Albanian words to try to conceal his identity. He behaved toward us detainees in an especially beastly way. He was very heavy-handed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can talk about that shortly, but for this moment, I'd like you to describe your final stop at Rajlovac and what happened upon your arrival there.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: As we were entering the bus, we had to sit down between the seats and put our heads between our knees. Sok made us sing Chetnik songs, starting the tune, which we had to take up and repeat, while two guards walked up and down the bus and hit us with police truncheons. And that went on all the way to Rajlovac. We were also stopped once near Reljevo, at the bridge, where a group of people were waiting for us, wanting to kill us. I don't know how long the argument lasted between the guards on our bus and those people, but in the end they didn't have their way and we went on. As we arrived at Rajlovac - we were between 10 and 15 - we were ordered to get off the bus in groups of five, to lie down outside the bus, again spread-eagled. And in Rajlovac we were met by people who were something like a "welcome party," arranged for us, very well prepared and experienced in the torture of detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Jahic. Could I just stop you there. And I'd like to produce to you a photograph bearing the number 00520200-11.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P367.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I noticed that on the description of the exhibit on the list, you already included part of I take it the testimony you expect, which is comment rather than a description of the -- the description should be limited to what appears and could be directly taken from the photograph. But in your description, especially the second part, is not something we could immediately see at this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I see, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, when we describe this exhibit, I'd like you to leave out the second part. I'd rather make a new description, saying that this is a photograph showing old iron and a cistern. Because whether the grid is correct, whether anyone was detained there is not something that appears on the photograph. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, you have the photograph before you.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise what you see in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. They are two hangars made of iron, metal, and that's where we were incarcerated. We spent from the 2nd of June, 1992, to the 14th of June, 1992 there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Jahic, if I could just containing you back to the point in the story that you were telling us. Does this photograph depict the location you were brought to at Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that, and in relation to the introduction of photographs, I would suggest that it's better to ask the witness what the photograph depicts as opposed to indicating to the witness and asking for an affirmative answer. I just put that as a marker for the introduction of further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, of course, if we ask the witness, then he'll start describing that as a hill in the photograph, that there's some old iron on it and -- so I would not say that, under these circumstances, it's not admissible. But I saw it this not as an objection, as a marker, but if you could always ask the witness, to the extent possible -- for example, by asking him whether he recognises this as a place he knows. And if he would then -- but that it is a place on the photograph, that doesn't need any further description by the witness. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've said that you were taken off the buses five at a time. Could you tell us from that point what you observed and what happened to you.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: We weren't able to see much because it was getting towards evening and dark. It was dusk. And five people, as they went out one by one, or five by five, they had to lie down in front of the bus, which was parked nearby the hangars, at a distance of about some 30 to 40 metres from the hangars. And in that "welcoming committee" or "welcoming party," the new torture or mistreatment being prepared for us -- I don't know how many Chetniks there were, but three of the people present were given the task of using their army boots to jump on our heads and legs, and our backs. And another two used metal rods to beat us with while we were lying down, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond face down. They beat us on our heads, across our backs, and on all parts of our bodies. Then one of them, one man from this group, would beat us on our soles, the soles of our feet, with a police truncheon, which was very painful indeed. And at one point, they brought in trained dogs, army dogs, and issued orders, gave them the command to bite us, which the dogs mostly did. Then one of the men present brought a fuel canister of some kind and they started soaking us with the fuel and intended to set fire to us. They asked us to admit to some nonsensical things, how many Mujahedins there were, how much Alija was paying us, and mindless things like that. And then they would continue torturing us. At one point they used a dredger and a caterpillar vehicle and wanted to run us over using those vehicles. But they didn't do that. I don't know how long this all went on for, an hour or two, perhaps more, this torture, and then we had to get up again and run the gauntlet of Chetniks, as I've already described. I described what this gauntlet looked like, ten or so people on one -- on either side, and we were beaten as we went through the gauntlet, with the instruments that I've already mentioned. We were told to run to the small hangar that you can see on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just, Mr. Jahic, now take you back again to describe this, as you put it, "welcoming committee." Did these people have any uniform on?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did have some sort of uniform. They were either camouflage uniforms or the blue uniforms that I described earlier on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this small hangar that you've mentioned, could you describe the hangar to us.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, it was of tin construction and it was used as a storehouse for different types of fuel with a top to it, after the fuel had been poured in. But this time the hangar had cut into it an entrance, two by two, for example, two by two metres. It had a door made of some iron netting. It was metal, anyway. And it was about ten metres in diameter. It was a steel construction. In my opinion, a hangar of this kind was re-adapted -- was adapted to serve as a prison camp where people could be incarcerated, where you could hold prisoners, because they had already prepared and staged everything, set the scene for the events that were to come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point, Mr. Jahic, I'd like to produce to you another document bearing the number RR045396.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P368.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we leave that particular photograph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- I think it would be important to -- if it could be indicated when the photograph was taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, do you have any information about the ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. The witness isn't aware of when the photograph was taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I think Ms. Loukas would like to know. So if you could provide that information to her, either now or -- I don't know whether there's any reason to do it in the absence of the witness, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I don't think there is. It was taken in 1997, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, just before, then, we leave this first picture, if I could direct the witness to have a look at this first picture again, 00520200-11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, could you please assist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, does this picture look to you as it did at the time you were at this location?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, the hangars are as they were, but otherwise none of this was there while we were there. So the answer is no. There are a lot of these vehicles about here. And that's not what it was like from the 2nd to the 14th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the hangars appear to you as they were in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go now to the second picture. Mr. Jahic, do you recognise anything in the second picture?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] Da.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you recognise?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: This is the small hangar, and my photograph. I was there when the photograph was taken, and I'm indicating the inside of the small silo, or rather, small hangar where I was detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you recognise the individual in that photo as yourself?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] Da.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us when, to the best of your recollection, that photo was taken.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it was at the end of 1996 or the beginning of 1997, but anyway, after the reintegration with the others, when we joined up with the people who came to get me. And we went down and took these photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this photograph, I see you're at an entrance to what appears to be the small hangar.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's it. That's the small hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a gate on either side of the entrance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the door or gate that I mentioned a moment ago, and that's what it looked like while we were kept in the hangar. They're made up of this metal grid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If we could go on, then. When you ran the gauntlet into the hangar, could you tell us what you saw once you got inside.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: As it was night-time, I wasn't able to see anything. The hangar is dark anyway inside, because there's no light coming into it. It's closed off. But we were ordered to run. And when I ran through the entrance gates, I fell across the other detainees who had been brought to the hangar earlier on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
