utterances.text: At a certain point, then, were you able to see approximately how many detainees were inside this hangar with you?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Not at night. But at dawn, visibility was better, and then I could see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were all people from Ahatovici, people who had been taken prisoner in Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of them come from any other settlements or areas outside of Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, there were some ten people whom I mentioned at the beginning of my statement from Bioca, and a couple of them from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jahic, you've said that you've stayed in that cistern until approximately 14 June. Could you tell us about some of the conditions inside that cistern. For example, how were you fed during your period of time in there?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, the conditions were, as they were in most camps in Bosnia-Herzegovina, held by the Chetniks. For the first five days, or first three or four days, actually, as far as I remember, we weren't given anything to eat at all. And then -- there were about a hundred of us in the hangar, and they threw in three loaves of stale bread. They were as hard as stone and had gone all green with mould. And this was generally repeated throughout my stay at the Rajlovac camp. The same thing happened again. We were given water regularly, but they didn't let us leave the hangar at all, go outside. Only when they tortured us and beat us up and Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond interrogated us. The conditions were extremely bad. It was very dirty. We had to urinate inside the hangar, using a bucket. And they didn't even let us empty the bucket. But when they were in a good mood -- except when they were in a good mood. So the stench was terrible. And throughout the time I spent in the hangar, I didn't need to defecate at all, because we weren't given any food to eat except for that mouldy bread, stale bread, with the clear intention of having the 100 of us fight over these three loaves of bread that they would throw to the dogs, as it were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry. Before Ms. Edgerton proceeds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder, in relation to that last answer, it commences with: "Well, the conditions were as they were in most camps in Bosnia-Herzegovina held by the Chetniks." It's not actually an answer to the question that Ms. Edgerton asked, and, Your Honour, I would submit it might be appropriate for Your Honours to indicate to the witness that it is appropriate for him to answer the question rather than to editorialise in the way that he did at the commencement of that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, I think we have to understand that there might be some emotion involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not know exactly what the source of that part of the testimony is. But if it's not substantiated to the effect that the witness saw them all, then of course the Chamber will not understand this part of the testimony to be anything else than just repeating what the witness may have heard or read or whatever. But, Mr. Jahic, Ms. Loukas is asking me to request you to, to the extent possible - and we do understand, of course, the circumstances under which you're testifying - but to concentrate mainly on your own experience. So when you compared the situation in your hangar with what happened elsewhere, we take it that you have no direct knowledge of how it was elsewhere and you may have some reasons to believe that elsewhere it wasn't any better. But we are very much interested to hear specifically what you experienced yourself, because that's the thing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear that last part of your answer. Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is that I was able to see through the information media, Batkovic camp, Trnopolje camp, and if they weren't identical to our camp, they were very similar to each other. So that would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So -- well, what I was mainly asking your attention for is to mainly concentrate on what you saw yourself, and of course I do understand that you might have compared your situation with what you have seen on the media. But that's, of course, not what you've personally experienced. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier, after your surrender you were ordered to strip to your underwear. Did you ever during your detention receive your clothing or your shoes again?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you -- at what point did you receive your clothing and shoes?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I omitted to say that all our valuables, any valuables we had on us, items of jewellery, gold jewellery, watches, money, was confiscated, either in Bojnik or Rajlovac. They searched us. So they didn't give us our shoes back. We did get our clothing back after five to six days after we were in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your detention in Rajlovac, Mr. Jahic, were you ever interrogated?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By whom, then, and where did this take place?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, the interrogation -- I was interrogated. Most of the other detainees were interrogated by Sok, with the assistance of two or three others, his assistants, Chetniks, who beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you abused during your interrogations?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, the whole time they got this -- these admissions from us by force, where the HOS were, where the Mujahedin were, how much we were being paid, where we were doing battle, and other nonsensical things like that. They made us say it and admit to things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic --

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: And along with that interrogation, while the interrogation was going on, we were beaten. We were beaten up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, did you also see any abuse of other prisoners in the same way?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the detainees in the small hangar camp were exposed to that kind of torture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe to us what you saw.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw on several occasions people being taken out. They took a man away. He was the father of a schoolmate of mine. And he was beastily beaten up on two occasions and died as a result in the small hangar camp, as a consequence of the beatings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. The name of that late individual was Mr. Hajro Delic. He was taken out twice. They came with an olive-green vehicle, a heavy-duty vehicle, with a pinzgauer, and took him away. And sometimes he'd be away the whole night. The second time he'd be aware for a shorter period of time. But when he returned to the camp, to the small hangar, and when they saw the state he was in, they just threw some sort of couch inside, and he was all black and blue. His ribs had been broken, his kidneys had probably been damaged, and his other internal organs. And Hajro Delic succumbed to his injuries and died, before our very eyes. All of us who were in the small hangar saw that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other instances where you saw similar abuse of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, Hajro Delic's case was not the only one. They also killed Enver Celik, for example. He also succumbed to that torture that he was subjected to, inhumane torture. And then all of us were tormented and mistreated. We were forced to go hungry. They even threw in some noxious matter into the hangar, poisonous gases and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period of your detention, Mr. Jahic, were there any examples of detainees being removed, never to be returned?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: There was a group -- there were people from Bioca. There were perhaps six or seven of them, that group. And then another group of the same number from Bratunac, for example. They were taken off in an unknown direction, and later on we learnt that some of those people had been killed. And also, in the period between the 9th and 14th of June, they took out nine people from Ahatovici, and we also later learnt that they were killed at Ilidza, where they were buried in the Vlahovo cemetery. And that was another case. If you want me to give you the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you remember the names of some of those people from Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: It was three members of the same Brajlovic family, Edin, Zijad, and another one, and Rusmir Pasic, Kadrija Ramadani, Dzemo Efendic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jahic. Now, you've mentioned before I interjected an incident where some kind of noxious substance was thrown into the hangar. Can you tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: I don't know which day of our stay at the camp it was, but one day there came a Chetnik whom I personally didn't know, but some of my fellow Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond inmates recognised him. And he brought some sort of device, like a bottle, and through the netted fence, he threw in this poison inside, with the words "breathe in, balijas. It's not a real bomb. Fuck your mothers." And what happened later is that those of us inside found ourselves in very stifling air. Our small blood vessels started bursting. We had a feeling that our lungs would implode. And we tried to breathe in more air, which had a completely different effect, because the air was already full of that substance. And we thought we were suffocating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, you've said that one of the other detainees recognised this individual. Who was it that recognised this individual?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: It was a friend of mine, a very close friend of mine and a former neighbour. He was a member of the reserve police force. And he recognised the said Chetnik as a former chauffeur and bodyguard for Krajisnik and Jovo Tintor. That Chetnik had arrived in an Audi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your friend's name?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: My friend's name is Armin Mujkic, late Armin Mujkic, I must say. He was killed in the bus massacre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your period of detention, were you ever asked to appear on camera?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. There was one occasion when this SRNA television from Pale arrived, and they took us out of the camp in groups of five or six detainees. They selected people who still looked normal, who were not disfigured by the beatings, and I was among these men. We received a piece of paper with a text that we were supposed to reproduce before the TV cameras. And this Chetnik nicknamed Sok told us all, before the filming, in so many words: Those of you who screw up will be killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move forward in time now to the 13th of June. What happened to you on that day?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of June, around 10.00 a.m., two refrigerator trucks belonging to UPI company from Rajlovac and the TP market, and parked outside the hangars, the small and the big one, and then the guards told us we were going to be transported to an exchange location. We had to board these refrigerator trucks. I don't know how we were divided, but I know that at that stage we were 56 in total. I don't know whether we were evenly distributed between the two hangars, 28 and 28. In any case, we were ordered to get onto the refrigerator trucks, and when we did, they closed the door behind us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you go further, could I just ask you one question. I note the number of detainees by this point in time had dropped from 100 to 56. Do you have any idea as to the reasons for that?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: The number dropped because, as I said, some of them had been killed at Ilidza, some had been killed in other locations. Yet another part had been transferred to the large hangar for some reason. So that from 100, the number dropped to around 56.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after they closed the door behind you in these refrigerated trucks, what then happened?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: When they drove us away, and at the time we didn't know where we were going, although we could look through a sliver-shaped opening for ventilation. We didn't have much air inside the truck, because the area inside was no bigger than 6 to 8 square metres, and there were too many of us inside. We didn't have enough air. Those of us who were younger and stronger could somehow stand it, but the older people who had previously been badly beaten took it very hard and moaned from pain throughout the trip. When the temperature rose to such a degree that it became insufferable, they would turn on the cooling, or rather, the freezing. So we had these temperature variations that were very ugly indeed. But we were able to follow through that slit where we were going, and we could see that first we arrived to the Vogosca hub, then to Semizovac, and then we continued along a by-road, a macadam road, and we only later learned that it was the road leading to Pale. The driver intentionally stepped hard on the gas so that the people with bad injuries literally moaned and cried from pain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could just for a moment, Your Honour. I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton. Yes. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Again, Ms. Edgerton, whether the itinerary of what the Chamber expects to be not the vital part of the -- whether that's really necessary. If you could perhaps take a bit more the lead, which is not the same as leading the witness. Then I have another issue I just briefly wanted to raise, is -- and perhaps we should go into private session for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I just may address the Trial Chamber before the witness comes into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with this witness, we still have to get to the core of his testimony. Following that, it's my intention to put a small number of intercept communications to him, perhaps three documents, and four video clips. Looking at the time and looking at the witness's overall condition at this point, I wanted to put the Trial Chamber on notice that what I would try and do is speed him up as much as possible to get to the core of his testimony, and then I would propose to play the video. Now, because the video is -- it's rather gruesome, frankly, Your Honour, and because, based on my long acquaintance with the witness, I see he appears to be rather drained now at this point of the day, I would ask the Trial Chamber if we could break after the video is played, until tomorrow morning, and then I would propose to play the intercepts first thing in the morning tomorrow in the most expeditious fashion possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we could do that, although we briefly discussed it, the testimony of this witness, during the last break, Ms. Edgerton, and the Chamber had the impression that if this witness was scheduled on Friday for the last two and a half hours until the weekend, that we might have had the whole of his testimony in a shorter period of time. There were a lot of details which, for example -- but we'll see how it develops. But at this moment, there's certainly not a negative reaction to your suggestion, mainly on the basis of the condition of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can indicate that -- nor do I have any objection to that course. It seems appropriate in the circumstances. And I would add, in any event, due to the situation that we don't have Ms. Cmeric here today and our inability to conduct the conferences as expeditiously as possible, we would not have been in a position to cross-examine at the end of the witness's evidence today in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any impression on how much time the cross-examination of this witness would take, approximately, knowing what still -- what there's still to be expected?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, of course, this week we have two witnesses who are scheduled. I must say from my perspective, Your Honour, I see no problem in our being able to deal with both witnesses well within time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Madam Usher, would you escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jahic, before the break, where we left off, you were telling us that you understood you were -- you found you were being taken in the refrigerated trucks on the road to Pale. Could you tell us where you stopped, just the name of the location.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: We stopped first at Pale, but only for a minute or two, before going on to Sokolac, where we stopped for about ten minutes, and then they brought us back to Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct, Mr. Jahic, that following your return through Pale, you were then brought back to Rajlovac barracks?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once at Rajlovac barracks, were you taken to the same place you had been detained or some other location?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: We were taken back to the small hangar, or rather, we were brought back to the larger hangar, where there were some men, other men, detainees. But we were ordered to go to the large hangar with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the large hangar empty at the time you arrived in it? Were there any other detainees there?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: It was empty when we returned from Pale. The large hangar was empty. There were no people inside. But they had poured water for us in the hangar. There were about 300 litres of water in the hangar, and the hangar itself was dug in somehow; the floor was a depression, so that water could be -- could stay there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, then, that you spent the night in that hangar but were removed later the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. There were -- the water was 30 centimetres deep on the ground of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: We were brought there around 7.00 and we stayed there until the next day, around 7.00, so we were there for about 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next day, were you taken to -- taken out of the hangar and taken to a bus?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of bus?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: It was, I believe, a bus that belonged to the Gras company from Sarajevo, a regular bus, red.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and the remaining detainees have to run another gauntlet to board that bus?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had to run the gauntlet again with our arms raised, and again we were hit on the way to the bus with all sorts of objects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any person from what you understood to be the camp authorities there?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw this Chetnik nicknamed Sok. I saw Mile Stojanovic, who was a military man. I don't know of which rank exactly, but he commanded over that barracks, or at least he held a high position there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you seen this person you call Mile Stojanovic prior to boarding the bus?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him up to ten times during the time I stayed at the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was he usually dressed when you saw him? Was he in uniform or civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: He was in uniform. Usually the blue fatigues worn by the air defence and air force men. I believe he had a Scorpio pistol as a side-arm. He held a rank, but I don't know which rank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jahic, once you and the other detainees boarded the bus, were you under guard? Were there any guards on the bus with you?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were some three to four guards, plus the bus driver. I want to add that when we set off, an escort made up of four vehicles followed the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of escort was that?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Armed men. As for vehicles, there was one green all-terrain vehicle called pinzgauer. Then there were two vehicles probably from the automobile factory in Vogosca. I think so because there were two completely new, brand new cars, one Zastava 101, and another car, also new, from the same factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was your position in the bus? Where were you sitting or standing?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: We were just cursed and told to go to the back of the bus. So we stood the greatest part of the trip, up to the Vogosca and Skapetla [phoen], the Vogosca hub, when we were ordered --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, were you in the front, the middle, or the rear of the bus?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: I was in the back of the bus, right next to the back windscreen, so I could see where we were going and I could see this escort, the VW Golfs and the Zastava vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened after you left the Vogosca junction.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Before they ordered us to lie down at Vogosca and Skapetla, I saw this car that was following us and the armed man in the car who wore this blue shirt, long, curly hair, and a cap turned sideways. And since he noticed that I was watching him, he motioned me to turn away, motioning that he would kill me otherwise. And so I obeyed. We were packed like sardines, practically lying on top of each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after you left --

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: And we were enough to fill two buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, what happened, then, after you were asked at the Vogosca junction to put your heads down?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: They kept driving us, for I don't know how long, stopping occasionally at an intersection, and on those occasions, the driver would receive some instructions, or maybe consulted with somebody, and then we would go on. And we were driven on that bus, packed as we were, which was very painful, because there was not a millimetre free space even to move your head, and anybody who would move would immediately be struck down by a rifle but the or a truncheon or a club. Because there were these armed, uniformed Chetniks guarding us on the bus. And after about an hour of this drive, the bus stopped and they said it was because the engine had started to boil.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just stop you for a moment there and ask you: Do you have any idea what road you had taken during this hour's worth of drive and where you were at this time?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: I think we were moving along the road from Sarajevo towards Olovo, and that stop that we made could have been at the intersection of the road to Ilijas and Semizovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after they said the engine had boiled?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: We were given orders not to move. They opened the front door and the escorts got out, as well as the bus driver. And one or two minutes later - I'm not sure exactly how much time went by - we could hear a very loud explosion. So that I couldn't hear for some time after that. And then there was one explosion, and a second one, and a third one, one after the other, and they were projectiles from hand held rocket launchers, whether Zoljas or some other type; I really can't say. When those three projectiles were fired, through the shattered windows, they started throwing in hand grenades, maybe ten hand grenades, along with firing from infantry weapons. I didn't have any idea how long this went on for and whether I was alive or dead, because there were explosions on all sides and I couldn't really make out whether they were shrapnels, bullets, body parts or whatever was flying around. At one point when I happened to raise my head up a bit, I saw a terrible sight all around me. I saw my friends with shattered heads, dismembered. There was blood all over me. There were parts of skulls, hair, all over me. And at that moment, I felt a terrible pain in my back. And since the shooting was still going on, I realised that I had been hit myself, and I saw several more hand grenades, or bombs, falling right next to me, in close proximity, and exploding underneath the body of some person, and the body was shattered. But it was so close to me, a metre and a half at the most away from me, that it was a terrible sight. You could hear screaming and moaning on the part of the people, you could smell the smell of burning, the smell of blood, gunpowder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, are you aware of or did you see anything happen to the people who had been guarding you on the bus, the guards from your bus, or the escort vehicles? And to your knowledge, were they shot or damaged in any way?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Absolutely nothing happened to those people. They were our hangmen. They were our executors. They shot at us. Chetniks and the Chetnik hordes conducting a massacre over unarmed people in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, while you were still on the bus, do you have any recollection of seeing or hearing any vehicles pass by?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: When the bus stopped at the place of the massacre, the site, when it stopped, we could hear two vehicles passing by on the right-hand side of the bus, to the right of the bus. And since the bus had stopped on the left-hand side of the road, the vehicles had to pass the bus, bypass it, on the right. And all this took place in the space of several minutes. The guards going out, the driver leaving the bus, the people who had guarded us, and the moment when these two vehicles passed by, vehicles that had been behind the bus to begin with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, were the vehicles you're talking about, were those part of the escort, the motorised escort you had?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the shooting had ended, were you then able to leave the bus somehow?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: I don't know how much time afterwards and how long it all went on for, because I lost all sense of time. I didn't know what to do, where I was, whether all that was actually happening to me, because the -- it was a terrible sight to behold. People with their heads blown off, they were close friends of mine; they were relatives and friends. But anyway, I managed somehow. When I was wounded, my legs had gone numb, but I managed somehow to pull myself out of there, with the help of my hands and arms. I was at the back of the bus, as I've already said, underneath the window frame and the handrails, and I managed to move through and move out and throw myself out of the bus, not to have to look at that terrible scene any more. When I tried to do that, as my legs were numb and I couldn't move them, I got wedged between the handrail and the window frame. I was stuck. And I was in limbo there for about ten minutes, stuck, until I mustered up the energy to catch hold of something, of the window frame, with my right hand and push with my left hand and tried to get my legs freed, and I somehow succeeded and fell out of the bus onto the road. And I hurt myself even worse doing that. And the pain and bleeding became much worse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, after you left the bus, were you somehow able to pull yourself to the side of the road?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: I wanted to get as far away from that place as possible, so I crawled backwards. I couldn't go forwards. I couldn't turn myself around, so I crawled and came to a nearby brook or stream, and I sat there thinking what had just happened. I thought I was going to die from the wounds that I had sustained. And I tried to kill myself, to put an end to my suffering and pain. I pulled out of my trousers a leather belt that I had. I put it round my head like this. I wound the other end around my right hand and I tried to strangle myself. But the whole thing bust and I fell into the stream. I crawled to the stream. The water was about half a metre high. I emerged [as interpreted] my head underneath the water, took a stone, and with my right hand, started hitting the back of my head, hoping to lose consciousness and to drown in the water. But I wasn't able to do that. I wasn't able to kill myself. I didn't succeed. And so once again I went back crawling to the bank of the stream.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jahic, while you were there, did you see or hear any vehicle come in the direction of the bus?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. After my attempt to kill myself, as I say, there was this bank or shore some two metres off. I was at the bottom of that embankment and you could hear the noise of a car at that moment, a car stopping next to the bus. And soon after that, a Chetnik got out wearing a camouflage uniform and holding an automatic rifle. He got in at the front door of the bus, where the driver and the escort had got off the bus prior to the massacre, and then just at random, randomly, he began shooting at the bodies of the people who were there, most probably he wanted to be 100 per cent certain that nobody remained alive, nobody from that group of 50 or 60 people. So he shot a burst of gunfire, two rounds of ammunition. And I watched this from a distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jahic, did you recognise the vehicle that that man you called the Chetnik came in? The vehicle you had seen before?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was one of the escort vehicles, Zastava 101, ivory coloured, off-white. And as I say, a man got out of it, wearing a camouflage uniform, a very largely built man, heavily built man, big man, with an automatic rifle. And then he proceeded to do what I just said. He fired two rounds of ammunition, two clips; then stood further away from the bus, threw in another two hand grenades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jahic --

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: -- for good measure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- what direction did that car come from?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: The car came from the direction that you take when you go to Pale, and we had gone that same way the previous day, when they took us to Pale and when he did what he came to do. He switched the motor on again and took off in the direction of Srednja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, is it correct that after -- sometime after observing this, you crawled back in the bus?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I managed somehow, although I was very seriously wounded, I dragged my legs behind me, that I had enough strength to break off two branches in a nearby bush. And as it had -- was raining that day, as it had been raining, I managed to pull myself out up over the embankment onto the road. And the reason why I wanted to go back was because I had heard some moans and cries from somebody who had been hit but who was still alive, who hadn't died straight away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you find anybody alive after you had crawled back onto the bus?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: No. Several moments later, I don't know how long afterwards; it took a long time. But when I did finally manage to reach the front door of the bus and haul myself up with the help of my hands and get inside, I started calling out to people, thinking that somebody had fallen on top of somebody else when there were the explosions. So I called out my own name and said: Can I help you? Is there anyone there? Can you help you? But just from time to time I would just hear a voice moaning for their mother, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, is it correct that you spent the night on that bus?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the night, did you hear or see any vehicles passing by?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] Da.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear or see?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: When I myself was wounded with fragmentation bullets, two of my ribs had been shattered. I couldn't find a comfortable position, but I managed to crawl to the driver's seat, and I thought that -- as it was a more comfortable seat, that I would be more comfortable. It was a foam upholstered seat. It took me a long time to haul myself up onto the seat. It was pitch dark. It was raining at one point. And then suddenly I heard a vehicle coming from the direction of Pale. It was a Golf, VW Golf vehicle, Golf II, I think it was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the vehicle stop?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: -- dark in colour. No, it didn't stop. But as it overtook the bus, the floodlights stopped me from seeing properly. I wasn't able to see properly. But I did manage to see that the car was dark in colour and that it was that particular vehicle, that make. And you could hear music coming out of the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you hear anything else?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: As the car passed by the bus, the co-driver, person sitting next to the driver, in front, he had his window open and he was sort of celebrating that a genocide and massacre had taken place. He celebrated by shooting two bullets up into the air as he passed by the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, do you know whether or not there were any other survivors besides yourself? And if so, how many?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: After the massacre itself, I managed to see that there were a couple of people who were not wounded as badly. Generally speaking, all those who had survived had been hit, more or less seriously, but they managed to jump out of the bus and go in the direction of the forest and take refuge in the forest and escape that way. Since I was seriously wounded myself, I wasn't able to go with them, I stayed; I remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, how many other survivors of this incident are there, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Another seven, which makes a total of eight. Eight of us survived out of the 50 or 60 detainees from the camp and hangar in Rajlovac, which means that 48 were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you suffer from any permanent disabilities now as a result of the injuries you received in this incident?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't able to move for a long time, for nine months. I was unable to walk. I was hit in my spine and in my legs. I am unfit for work and a 100-per cent invalid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that following the reintegration of the municipality of Novi Grad, subsequent to the Dayton Peace Agreement, you returned to live in Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Like most of the inhabitants of Ahatovici, we all went back to our homesteads where we lived before the war. Although in 1992, the aim was to cleanse the area, ethnically speaking, because everybody was expelled from Ahatovici and Dobrosevici, all the Muslims, and even some Serbs as well. They were expelled too if they were in a mixed marriage, for example. And the mosque was destroyed. And while I myself was in the camp, the Chetnik Sok bragged and boasted that he had blown up the mosque and that the mosque was very solid and strong and that he had to blow it up twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This would, but for the reference to the exhibits that I've referred to previously, conclude the testimony in chief. I note the time, and I could advise the Trial Chamber that were we to view the video clips themselves immediately, although they're not long at all, the clips would probably take us right up to 1.45 this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And would you have then any additional questions in relation to those clips or just perhaps tomorrow or what would you prefer to do?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have some additional questions. I would be asking for the witness's comment, of course, and what he's seen. My preference would be to play this first thing in the morning, in, as I said, as expeditious a manner as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you'd rather adjourn now and to play it tomorrow morning. And you do not fear that what then remains could be influenced by perhaps the impact viewing the video might have on the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, there's less chance of that if we do it all tomorrow, in one block.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I leave it up to you, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn for the day. And we'd like to see you back, Mr. Jahic, tomorrow morning at 9.00. I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you've given until now, and neither about testimony still to be given tomorrow. We will be in this same courtroom tomorrow morning. So we'll adjourn until 9.00 tomorrow morning.
